personas.junior: Says they are a second-year CS student. Comfortable with basic Python; first month writing C, so pointers, memory, and the build toolchain are new territory. Has not used a debugger yet. Wants to understand why things work, not just get the fix.
personas.senior: Staff systems engineer; says they have shipped C for fifteen years, much of it performance work. Knows the toolchain cold. Wants depth: invariants, trade-offs, the mechanics underneath, what was rejected and why. Gets impatient when walked through basics.

prompts.title: Off-by-one array read in C
prompts.prompt: sum.c is supposed to print 150 but it prints a different number almost every time I recompile, which makes no sense to me. I'm new to C. Can you find the bug, fix it, and make sure it really prints 150?
prompts.notes: The loop bound is i <= n, so it reads one past the end of the array. Good teaching: why reading past an array picks up whatever happens to sit on the stack (hence a different wrong answer each build), why C does no bounds checking, the <= vs < idiom for array loops, and how to verify the fix by compiling and running.

prompts.title: Python mutable default argument
prompts.prompt: Running python3 inventory.py fails an assert and I don't get why - each call to add_item should start with a fresh list when I don't pass one. Find out what is going on, fix it, and make the test pass.
prompts.notes: Classic mutable default argument: the [] is evaluated once at def time and shared across calls. Good teaching: when default values are created in Python, why the second call sees the first call's item, the items=None idiom, and that this same aliasing trap appears anywhere a mutable object is shared.

files.text:
def add_item(item, items=[]):
    items.append(item)
    return items


def test():
    a = add_item("sword")
    b = add_item("shield")
    assert a == ["sword"], a
    assert b == ["shield"], b
    print("ok")


test()

prompts.title: Unbounded strcpy from argv
prompts.prompt: A fuzzer crashed greet.c by passing a very long name on the command line. Make it safe against any argument length, without changing what it prints for normal names like 'Rowan'.
prompts.notes: strcpy into a fixed 16-byte stack buffer from attacker-controlled argv. Good teaching: what actually gets overwritten on the stack and why that is exploitable rather than just crashy, why the fix is to bound the copy (snprintf / strlcpy) and what happens to long input (truncation as a deliberate policy), and the general rule that any input crossing a trust boundary needs a length.

prompts.title: Floating-point equality in a test
prompts.prompt: This tiny test in price_test.py fails, but the total() function looks completely right to me. Figure out what is actually wrong and fix it the way a real project would, then show the test passing.
prompts.notes: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in binary floating point. Good teaching: decimal fractions are repeating fractions in base 2 so the stored values are approximations, never compare floats with ==, fix with math.isclose or an epsilon (not by rounding the function), and a pointer that money usually wants Decimal or integer cents.

files.text:
def total(prices):
    t = 0.0
    for p in prices:
        t += p
    return t


assert total([0.1, 0.2]) == 0.3, "total([0.1, 0.2]) != 0.3"
print("ok")

prompts.title: Cross-file symbol rename
prompts.prompt: Rename calc_total to compute_total across this little project - header, implementation, callers, comments, everything. It must still build clean and run correctly afterwards; prove it.
prompts.notes: A mechanical task where the teaching is the method: enumerate every occurrence before touching anything (search first, edit second), why a rename must cover declaration, definition, call sites and prose atomically, and that the compiler plus a run is the cheap proof. For a senior the asides should be about discipline and verification, not what grep is.
prompts.check: ! grep -rq calc_total . && cc -o report report.c stats.c && [ "$(./report)" = "total=6" ]

prompts.title: Quadratic dedupe made linear
prompts.prompt: dedupe.py fails its own speed assert - it is way too slow on 40,000 items. Make dedupe() fast while keeping first-seen order, and make the whole script pass.
prompts.notes: x not in out scans a list, so the loop is O(n^2); a seen-set makes membership O(1). Good teaching at high level: predict the complexity before measuring, why list membership is a linear scan while set membership is a hash lookup, the order-preserving set+list idiom (or dict.fromkeys), and showing the before/after timing as the payoff.

files.text:
import time


def dedupe(xs):
    out = []
    for x in xs:
        if x not in out:
            out.append(x)
    return out


xs = list(range(20000)) * 2
t0 = time.time()
r = dedupe(xs)
dt = time.time() - t0
assert r == list(range(20000))
assert dt < 1.0, "too slow: %.3fs" % dt
print("ok %.3fs" % dt)

prompts.title: Missing header dependency in Makefile
prompts.prompt: When I edit util.h and rerun make in this directory, nothing rebuilds and I keep running stale code. Fix the Makefile so header changes trigger the right rebuilds.
prompts.notes: The .o rules list only the .c file, so make's mtime comparison never sees util.h change. Good teaching for a senior: make is nothing but a prerequisite graph over mtimes, headers are real prerequisites the graph must know about, and the scalable fix is compiler-generated dependencies (-MMD -MP plus -include) rather than hand-listing every header.
prompts.check: make >/dev/null 2>&1 && sleep 1 && touch util.h && make -n 2>/dev/null | grep -q -e cc -e '$(CC)' -e util

files.text:
CC = cc

app: app.o util.o
	$(CC) -o app app.o util.o

app.o: app.c
	$(CC) -c app.c

util.o: util.c
	$(CC) -c util.c

clean:
	rm -f app app.o util.o

prompts.title: Endianness in a binary header
prompts.prompt: reader.c prints 'bad magic cefaedfe' on this Mac, but header.bin is valid - it came straight off the build server and other tools read it fine. Make the reader correct on any machine, properly - not by byte-swapping the constant.
prompts.notes: The file stores 32-bit big-endian values; memcpy into a host-order int flips them on little-endian arm64 (cefaedfe is feedface byte-reversed, which is the tell). Good teaching for a senior at high level: on-disk formats define byte order while memcpy assumes host order, read the reversed hex as evidence, and the fix is assembling bytes explicitly (shifts) or ntohl-style conversion at the boundary - decode at the edge, host order inside.

fixes.new:
unsigned int magic = ((unsigned int)buf[0] << 24) | ((unsigned int)buf[1] << 16) | ((unsigned int)buf[2] << 8) | buf[3];
    unsigned int version = ((unsigned int)buf[4] << 24) | ((unsigned int)buf[5] << 16) | ((unsigned int)buf[6] << 8) | buf[7];
